observation: Transaction throughput is critically affected by the order in which conflicting transactions execute, yet practical systems generally process transactions in FIFO order and resolve conflicts reactively, and recent scheduling techniques explore only a small subset of possible schedules. The resulting performance gap is large and systematic: for a batch of four conflicting transactions one schedule can reduce makespan by 25% over another, the gap grows arbitrarily for larger workloads, and on real workload traces FIFO can increase makespan over optimized schedules by 43.2% for Epinions, 8.0% for SmallBank, 96.2% for TAOBench, 101.6% for TPC-C, and 99.3% for YCSB. Finding an optimal schedule is NP-complete, and existing heuristics sacrifice schedule quality for efficiency.

solution.idea: Prior work is stuck between two extremes: conflict-reactive protocols let lock acquisition, wait queues, and validation order choose a schedule without ever inspecting the batch as a whole, while deterministic systems choose a simple chronological order that must be replicated identically but is not chosen to minimize makespan. Exact makespan optimization is NP-complete, and single-pass greedy list scheduling sacrifices quality because it commits to one arbitrary ordering. The direction I propose is to insert a planning layer between transaction admission and concurrency control, and to make the plan itself the input to the execution engine. The planning problem is expressed on the conflict graph of the admitted batch: each transaction is a vertex; an undirected edge means the two transactions have a read/write or write/write conflict. A schedule is represented as an ordered list of color classes, where each color class is an independent set of the conflict graph. Transactions in the same class run concurrently because they are pairwise conflict-free, while classes run one after another, so conflicting transactions are serialized across class boundaries. With estimated transaction processing times, the makespan of a candidate schedule is the sum, over classes, of the maximum estimated duration inside that class. This maps the problem directly onto graph coloring, which the related work identifies as the core NP-complete decision, but it adds processing-time weights to the colors. The core insight is that we should not try to avoid NP-hardness by using a single greedy coloring; instead, we should treat schedule quality and computation time as a tunable trade-off inside a bounded anytime planner. The planner first produces a good weighted-DSATUR coloring, then explores many alternatives with beam search, and finally improves the current incumbent with local color moves and color-class merges; for small batches it runs an exact branch-and-bound search with clique-based lower bounds. This explores a much larger subset of possible schedules than FIFO, lock-queues, or timestamp order, and it can be stopped at any time while still returning a feasible schedule whose quality is monotonically improving. The trade-offs I considered and rejected were: modifying the lock manager to choose winners greedily at each conflict, which lacks a global objective; using only critical-path serial orders, which ignores the opportunity to run independent transactions concurrently; and invoking a general-purpose exact solver on every batch, which is intractable for large conflict graphs. The proposed design instead uses the conflict graph as an explicit first-class input and makes the search cost explicit through beam width, number of local-search iterations, and an exact-search threshold.
solution.implementation: The implementation is a scheduling and execution pipeline composed of five interacting parts: batch admission, conflict-graph construction, weighted schedule search, schedule enforcement, and duration estimation. Part 1, batch admission: each arriving transaction is placed in an admission buffer instead of being submitted directly to the lock manager. The scheduler forms a window of at most W transactions, or waits at most a time budget T before closing the window. Planning for the next window proceeds in the background while the current window executes, so the search does not add latency when W and the search budget are small. Part 2, conflict-graph construction: for each transaction i in the window, the planner obtains a declared or conservatively inferred read set R_i and write set W_i, and an estimated uncontended duration p_i. Read sets and write sets are gathered from stored-procedure declarations, from predicate analysis, or from the previous executions of the same transaction class. An undirected conflict edge is added between i and j whenever their access sets overlap with at least one write, that is, when (R_i intersect W_j) union (W_i intersect R_j) union (W_i intersect W_j) is nonempty. If access sets cannot be known exactly, the planner uses conservative predicates; any conflict that is still missed is not a correctness problem because the underlying concurrency-control engine remains in place as a backstop. Part 3, schedule representation and objective: a feasible schedule is a partition of the transactions into an ordered sequence of color classes C_1, C_2, ..., C_k such that every class is an independent set of the conflict graph. The cost of the schedule is makespan(C_1,...,C_k) = sum over classes c of max over transactions i in C_c of p_i. This cost function is what makes the coloring objective-aware: equal-duration transactions reduce to ordinary graph coloring, but unequal durations encourage the planner to put short transactions into already expensive classes rather than creating a new class. Part 4, weighted schedule search: the search has four stages. Stage 4a constructs an initial incumbent using a weighted DSATUR greedy. Transactions are sorted in nonincreasing p_i, breaking ties by descending conflict degree. Each transaction is placed into the first compatible existing color class that minimizes the marginal increase max(0, p_i - max(p_u for u already in class)); if no compatible class exists, a new class is opened. This single pass is fast and provides an upper bound. Stage 4b is a beam search over partial colorings. Starting from an empty schedule, the algorithm processes one uncolored transaction at a time. For each partial schedule, the next transaction is chosen among the uncolored vertices, preferring the vertex with the largest number of neighbors already colored. For every existing color class that is compatible with that vertex, a successor is created by placing the vertex in that class; one additional successor is created by opening a new class. Each successor is evaluated by its current cost. After expanding all partial schedules in the frontier, only the B successors with the smallest current cost are kept. Since the cost of a partial coloring is monotonically nondecreasing when later vertices are added, a partial schedule whose cost already equals or exceeds the incumbent makespan is discarded. Stage 4c improves the incumbent with local search. For each color class whose maximum defines its contribution, the planner repeatedly tries three move families: single-vertex moves, pair swaps, and class merges. A single-vertex move removes transaction i from class C_a and tries every compatible class C_b, accepting the move if the total cost does not increase and recording the best improving move. A pair swap exchanges two vertices between two classes when both classes remain independent after the swap. A class merge takes two color classes whose union is still independent and replaces them by one class, which strictly reduces the number of class contributions. The local search loops for L iterations or until no improving move is found; if it converges early, the planner performs a bounded number of restarts with perturbed processing-time estimates to escape local minima, keeping the best feasible schedule as the output. Stage 4d handles small windows exactly. If the number of transactions in the window is at most a threshold N_exact, the planner invokes a depth-first branch-and-bound search instead of only the beam and local stages. The state of that search is a partial coloring and its current cost. The next uncolored transaction with the highest degree to colored vertices is chosen; successors are generated by placing it in any compatible existing class or in a new class. A successor is pruned when its current cost is at least the incumbent cost or when current cost plus an admissible residual lower bound is at least the incumbent. The residual lower bound is obtained by finding a clique in the residual conflict graph and summing the estimated durations of that clique, because every member of a clique must occupy a distinct color class and therefore must contribute its own duration to the final makespan. When the exact search completes, it returns the optimal weighted coloring, and when it times out it returns its best incumbent instead. Part 5, schedule enforcement and execution: the final schedule is passed to the concurrency-control executor as an ordered list of color classes. For class C_1, all transactions in that class are dispatched to the database worker pool and run under the existing concurrency-control protocol, normally two-phase locking or optimistic concurrency control. Once all transactions in C_1 have committed, class C_2 starts, and so on. Since C_j is independent in the known conflict graph, there should be no modeled lock conflicts within a class; if a missed conflict causes a lock wait, the existing concurrency-control engine resolves it while preserving correctness, and the actual class duration is observed and recorded. For deterministic database execution, every replica runs the same deterministic search procedure on the same conflict graph, the same duration estimates, and the same fixed random seed, so all replicas produce the same color schedule and replay it in the same class order; this is consistent with the deterministic-ordering requirement but replaces arrival-timestamp order with a makespan-aware order. Part 6, adaptive duration estimates: after a transaction commits, the executor records its measured duration and updates the stored duration estimate for its transaction class using an exponential moving average, so future conflict graphs and schedules use better weights. Key parameters are W, the scheduling-window size; T, the maximum time before a partial window is closed; B, the beam width; L, the maximum number of local-search iterations; N_exact, the largest window size for which exact branch-and-bound is attempted; and a time budget for the planner. These parameters are exposed as configuration knobs, allowing a deployment to trade schedule-quality search effort against planning latency. The planner always keeps its best feasible schedule, so even when the search budget is exhausted it returns a valid schedule, and the output improves monotonically as B, L, or the time budget grows.
